items.content:
Flashback to June 14, 2024.

At the time, frontier AI models have zero fluid intelligence. They score around 5% on ARC 1. They can't reliably add two numbers. They make laughable logic errors every other prompt. Reasoning models don't exist. Coding agents don't exist. Claude Code doesn't exist. "Code gen" is a complete joke. Scaling up next-token prediction based on web text data is hitting a wall.

What if a time traveler told you that, by November 2026...

• AI models would have human-like fluid intelligence, thanks to a new paradigm: test-time induction (modern reasoning models).
• Not only would ARC 1 be saturated, but unreleased benchmarks 10x harder (ARC 2) and 100x harder (ARC 3) would be saturated too.
• Nearly all code would be written by AI, and models could one-shot complex codebases flawlessly.
• AI models would be solving multiple Millennium Prize problems.
• OpenAI's valuation would be 15x higher, and Anthropic's would be 85x higher.

And on top of all that...

• Nvidia would still hold ~80% of the AI compute market.
• Nvidia would have grown its revenue and earnings 4.5x.
• Nvidia would still be growing 75% a year.
• Nvidia would have even higher operating margins (67% vs. 65% back then).

Based on that information, straight from the future, would you have bought NVDA?

If you answered yes -- congrats. Today, 2.5 years later, you'd be down 5% on your investment (even more after inflation).

AI downloads broke the usual CDN model

Since this summer, we're running our own CDN at Hugging Face...
items.content:
AI downloads broke the usual CDN model

Since this summer, we're running our own CDN at Hugging Face. It's shipping almost 1 exabyte per month, which means, in practice, about 420 GB every second, through 80,000 requests per second.

Why did we need to build our own?

Well, CDNs were designed to ship many small web files to many people. AI downloads are pretty different: it's a few enormous files, a significant part of them pulled by machines.

This changes a lot of design assumptions.

You're not caching small objects close to users in hundreds of cities anymore: these users are for a big part GPU clusters sitting in a handful of cloud regions.

And a cached web page is useful to 1,000 visitors, while a cached 1,000 GB model is useful to far fewer clients, but each one wants all of it, immediately.

So we've built our own CDN, with caches adapted to massive objects, able to handle release-day mega-floods and multiple giant datasets and trending models being pulled at once.

The team made a live map of it at https://t.co/hx0ZISQWDo

Hard to stop watching it - it's quite mesmerizing

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Claude may have just solved the Riemann hypothesis, math's most famous unsolved problem, 167 years after it was first posed.

@__alpoge__ , a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a 4-page note saying he found the proof "working with Claude," and that the same method proves the generalized Riemann hypothesis

• He says he chose the direction and Claude did much of the hard technical work, especially near the finish line

• The full argument ran past 250,000 pages, so he released it only as Lean code, split into 14 files a computer can check line by line

• MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland says he independently checked it in Lean and called it "an historic moment"

• It's a Millennium Prize Problem with a $1M bounty

• On the same day, a separate 940-page GRH draft by Alessandro Masullo surfaced, written over 12 years with no AI and reviewed for months by Stanford's Brian Conrad

@theojaffee: "There's a timeline here where Levent says it was actually November 16th, GRH, the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which means we actually did get Riemann hypothesis before GTA VI. By 3 days."

items.title: Parallel Search scores 83 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index, level with Keenable Search (pro) ...
items.content:
Parallel Search scores 83 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index, level with Keenable Search (pro) at the top of the board, with a fast mode at 82 for $0.014 per task

We benchmarked two modes of @p0's Parallel Search API, fast and advanced, in our Stirrup agent harness with Parallel Search as its web_search tool to complete 1700 search-focused tasks.

In our August runs, advanced scored 75 and fast scored 73. In these November runs, advanced scores 83 and fast scores 82.

Key benchmarking results for Parallel Search:

➤ Artificial Analysis Search Index: Parallel Search (advanced, objective) scores 83, 1st of 26, and Parallel Search (fast, objective) 82, 4th. That is a ~50-point lift over the same model with no search (33). Advanced is level with Keenable Search (pro) at 83 and 3 points ahead of Exa (auto, dynamic highlights) and Perplexity (medium) at 80. Fast is slightly ahead of both

➤ DeepSearchQA is Parallel's strongest benchmark: both modes score 89 F1, 1st and 2nd of 26, comparable to Keenable Search (pro) at 88. Advanced also ranks 1st on AA-Omniscience (74%), just ahead of Keenable Search (pro) (73%), and 3rd on BrowseComp (87%, level with Keenable Search (pro) and Perplexity (medium))

➤ Low cost: fast costs about $0.014 per task, 2nd lowest of 26 behind TinyFish ($0.009), against a board median of $0.063. Advanced costs about $0.030 per task, 6th lowest

Key details:

➤ Setup: GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) in Stirrup, Parallel Search API with mode=fast and mode=advanced

➤ Tool shape: the model fills Parallel's objective (optional) and search_queries (1 to 3) fields on each call

➤ Pricing: $1 per 1k requests (fast) and $5 per 1k requests (advanced)

items.content:
Math Academy's @justinskycak argues that AI doesn't level the playing field between beginners and experts, even in math. It raises the ceiling for everyone:

A 1/10 can become a 10. But a 10/10 can become a 100.

"It's easy to think that because a tool can do stuff for you, it's taken away from me the opportunity to do things. But in reality, if you have a lot of expertise, this tool can extend you in ways. It's a multiplier on you."

"Having a calculator doesn't mean that you don't need to know what you're doing anymore. It means that when you know what you're doing, you can do more of it faster and extend it."

"LLMs is this very similar kind of setup, but just to software in general and domain expertise in general."

"The more you know what you're doing, the more you see the surface area of all these problems to solve with the LLM, and what problems are worth solving."

"If your skill level used to be a 1 out of 10 and now with the AI it's like, 'Oh, I'm a 10 out of 10.' Well, guess what? The scale's out of 100 now. If you were a 10 out of 10, you become 100."
@_MathAcademy_

items.content:
Hot take on the possible solution to Riemann:

1. The result is incredibly impressive if it holds up. (But see tweet below, it’s scarcely been diligenced.)

2. Anyone who is intellectually serious and interested in AI and math should (re)read my essay “AlphaProof, AlphaGeometry, ChatGPT, and why the future of AI is neurosymbolic” from July 2024, which lavished praise on DeepMind for exploring neurosymbolic models that are predecessors to the systems that Alpöge used with Riemann, and explained (correctly) why pure LLMs could not the same. (Pure LLMs still can’t.)

https://t.co/YYGDIrpnCp

If you think the progress on Riemann is a challenge to me rather than a confirmation of what I have argued for 25 years, you have the argument backwards.

3. The new result has not yet been confirmed yet, just to be clear.

4. But even it is confirmed, it wouldn’t much change the problematic economics of generative AI, because the particular techniques that it relies on involve elaborate symbolic theorem proving techniques that aren’t generally applicable to everyday reasoning. (It’s probably;y more like Deep Blue winning in chess in 1997: a special-purpose symbolic system that was wildly impressive but lacked general applicability.)

5. For more, my 2020 article in the The Next Decade in AI explained why advances in neurosymbolic AI alone would not be enough to get to robust intelligence, and I think what I said there still holds.

items.title: A free online book: Statistical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning: A Non-Asymptotic Perspective ...
items.content:
A free online book: Statistical Foundations of Reinforcement Learning: A Non-Asymptotic Perspective by Yuxin Chen, Yuejie Chi, Jianqing Fan, Gen Li, Yuting Wei, and Yuling Yan (2026).

The book develops a rigorous account of how much data reinforcement-learning algorithms need to estimate values and learn effective policies.

Centered on finite-state, finite-action Markov decision processes, the book studies finite-sample and finite-time performance, including settings where data are scarce.

Its mathematical treatment draws on probability, statistics, information theory, and statistical learning theory, and presents largely self-contained proofs with intermediate arguments intended to build intuition. 

Readers interested in the theory and analysis of reinforcement learning will find a sustained comparison of algorithms’ guarantees and the fundamental limits those guarantees are measured against.

The book is technical, so read it after you read my https://t.co/QTUJV5JXGK which is technical too, but in a manageable way.

Inkling 2 Mini uses ~38% more output tokens than Qwen3.8 27B for the same Intelligence Index score, but ~2.8x less compute.

Twelve of its 24 layers run three times per token, adding compute without adding output tokens. It averages ~152K output tokens per Intelligence Index task vs. ~110K for Qwen3.8 27B and ~158K for Nanbeige4.3-33B. • This is great if you are building an agent that requires real-time lookups.

• Servers are dynamically scaled up and down by the platform.

You can still use their classic input interface. It's cheaper and the better option for big batch jobs, but the new one is great for frequent calls.

SITUATION EXPLAINED: A new pancreatic cancer treatment stopped tumor growth in 90% of patients in an early trial, offering new hope against one of the deadliest cancers.

• Revolution Medicines' daily pill, RASONQUE (daraxonrasib), was tested alongside chemotherapy in 61 patients with previously untreated metastatic pancreatic cancer

• Tumors shrank or disappeared in 60.7% of patients, with 8.2% showing no detectable tumors on scans

• The treatment achieved a 90.2% disease control rate, with patients going a median of 12.8 months before their cancer progressed

• The drug targets RAS proteins that drive cancer growth, a pathway involved in more than 90% of pancreatic cancers

• The results come from an early Phase 1/2 trial. A larger Phase 3 trial is underway to establish how the combination compares with standard chemotherapy

@sophiadew
: "We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer, which is so long overdue."
